issue.issue_text: Whether the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970 (President's Act 19 of 1970) ceased to have effect upon the revocation of the Proclamation under Article 356 of the Constitution, thereby making the petitioner's continued detention unlawful.

facts: The petitioner was detained under the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970, which was a President's Act.
This Act was enacted by the President while a Proclamation under Article 356 of the Constitution (President's Rule) was in effect in West Bengal.
The Proclamation was later revoked by the President.

The petitioner's counsel argued that upon the revocation of the Proclamation, the President's Act automatically ceased to have effect, making the petitioner's continued detention under that Act unlawful.
law: The Court relied on Article 357(2) of the Constitution.
This clause specifies that any law made by the President or Parliament during a period of President's Rule (under Article 356) does not immediately become void when the Proclamation is revoked.
Instead, such a law continues to be in force until it is altered, repealed, or amended by the competent State Legislature.
The text explicitly states that such a law will cease to have effect one year after the proclamation has ceased to operate, unless it is sooner repealed or re-enacted by the state legislature.
application: The Court found the petitioner's argument to be based on the incorrect assumption that a law made by the President during a Proclamation ceases to operate immediately upon the revocation of that Proclamation.
The Court stated that this assumption runs directly contrary to the provisions of Article 357(2) of the Constitution.
It clarified that the period for which a law made under Article 356 remains in force is not co-terminous with the duration of the Proclamation itself.
Therefore, the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970, remained in force despite the revocation of the Proclamation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's contention, holding that, in accordance with Article 357(2) of the Constitution, the President's Act No. 19 of 1970 did not cease to have effect upon the revocation of the Proclamation. The Act would remain in force for one year after the Proclamation ceased to operate unless repealed or re-enacted by the state legislature. Consequently, the petitioner's detention under the Act was still lawful.

issue.issue_text: Whether the grounds of detention, which included hurling bombs and the recovery of high explosive bombs from the petitioner's possession, were germane to the object of maintaining public order under the Act.

facts: The petitioner was detained under the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970, for acting in a manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order.

The grounds for detention cited two incidents: (1) The petitioner and his associates hurled bombs, which created panic and injured a guard. (2) High explosive bombs and materials were later recovered from the petitioner's possession.
law: Under Section 3(2)(d) of the Act, "acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order" includes committing an offense under the Explosive Substances Act, 1908, where such an offense "disturbs, or is likely to disturb, public order."
The object of detention under the Act is preventive, meaning it is to prevent a person from acting in a manner prejudicial to public order.
application: The Court first analyzed the incident of hurling bombs (February 12, 1971) and found that it clearly disturbed public order and created panic, thus falling within the scope of the Act.

The Court then addressed the recovery of high explosive bombs (February 23, 1971). It reasoned that while the bombs were recovered before they could be used, their possession constituted an offense under the Explosive Substances Act.
The Court determined that the use of such bombs is inherently "likely to disturb public order."

It rejected the argument that the bombs had to be used for the grounds to be valid. The Court pointed to the earlier bomb-hurling incident as evidence of the petitioner's "propensity" to use such weapons.

The Court emphasized the preventive nature of the detention, stating that the recovery of the bombs simply prevented the petitioner from disturbing public order, which is the goal of the Act. The detention was justified to prevent future acts based on his past conduct and possession of bombs.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the grounds for detention were germane to the purpose of maintaining public order. The past act of hurling bombs and the subsequent possession of high explosive bombs (which he had a propensity to use) were sufficient to justify the preventive detention order under the Act.

issue.issue_text: Whether the impugned detention order was not in conformity with section 10 of the Act because it did not specify the date of detention.

facts: The petitioner argued that the detention order was invalid because it did not specify the date of detention.

This argument was based on the wording of Section 10 of the Act, which requires the government to place the case before an Advisory Board "within thirty days from the date of detention under the order".
law: The Court interpreted the phrase "from the date of detention under the order" to mean the date of the *commencement* of the detention, which is when the person is actually taken into custody.
The Court found that there is nothing in Section 10 that makes it obligatory for the detaining authority to specify the date of detention in the order itself.
application: The Court reasoned that it is often difficult for the detaining authority to know in advance the exact date a person will be taken into custody.
The person ordered to be detained might abscond or conceal themselves, delaying their apprehension.
If the petitioner's argument were accepted, the detention order would become unenforceable if the person could not be apprehended on the specific date mentioned in the order.
The Court found it difficult to draw such an inference from the language of the Act.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petitioner's argument, concluding that the detention order was not required to specify the date of detention. The 30-day period mentioned in Section 10 begins from the actual date the person is taken into custody, not from a pre-determined date in the order.

cases.case_name: The Supreme Court relied on the following legal principle without citing a specific case
cases.principle: If the past conduct and antecedents of a person reveal a tendency to act in a manner prejudicial to public order, an order of detention would be upheld, even if public order is not actually disturbed due to some supervening cause like prompt police action.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A law enacted by the President during a Proclamation under Article 356 does not cease to operate immediately upon the revocation of the Proclamation; pursuant to Article 357(2), such a law remains in force for one year after the Proclamation ends, unless it is repealed or re-enacted sooner by the appropriate legislature. Furthermore, a detention order is valid if based on the person's past conduct and antecedents which suggest a tendency to act in a manner prejudicial to public order, even if a disturbance is ultimately prevented by a supervening cause. The statutory period of detention commences from the actual date of apprehension, not from a date specified in the order.
obiter: It is not necessary to consider the legal position regarding subsisting detentions after the Act ceases to have effect in accordance with Article 357(2) of the Constitution.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The petitioner's detention is lawful. The West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970, did not cease to operate upon the revocation of the President's Proclamation, due to the saving provision in Article 357(2) of the Constitution. The grounds for detention, involving the possession and use of high explosive bombs, were germane to the maintenance of public order as defined by the Act, because the petitioner's past conduct revealed a tendency to commit such acts. Finally, the detention order was not invalid for failing to specify the date of detention, as Section 10 of the Act does not impose such an obligation, referring instead to the date the person is actually taken into custody.
legal_tests_applied: Article 357(2) of the Constitution: A law made by the President in exercise of the power of the Legislature of a State during a Proclamation under Article 356 continues in force even after the Proclamation is revoked, until it is altered, repealed, or re-enacted by the appropriate Legislature.

Section 3(2)(d) of the West Bengal (Prevention of Violent Activities) Act, 1970: The expression "acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order" includes the commission of an offence under the Explosive Substances Act, 1908, when the commission of such offence disturbs or is likely to disturb public order.

Preventive Detention Standard: To detain a person to prevent them from acting prejudicially to public order, it is sufficient that the detaining authority considers it necessary based on past conduct and antecedents revealing a tendency to do such acts, even if public order is not actually disturbed due to a supervening cause like police action.

Statutory Interpretation of Section 10: The phrase "from the date of detention under the order" refers to the date the detention actually commences when the person is taken into custody, and does not create an obligation for the detaining authority to specify that date in the detention order itself.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the President's Act ceased to have effect upon the revocation of the Proclamation was rejected because it was based on an incorrect assumption that runs contrary to clause (2) of Article 357 of the Constitution, which keeps such laws in force until repealed or re-enacted by the appropriate legislature.

The contention that the grounds were not germane to public order failed because the petitioner's actions, including possessing high explosive bombs, constituted an offence under the Explosive Substances Act, which is explicitly included in the definition of acting in a manner prejudicial to public order under Section 3(2)(d) of the Act. The petitioner's past conduct showed a propensity to use such bombs.

The argument that the detention order was invalid for not specifying the date of detention was dismissed because the court found nothing in Section 10 of the Act that makes it obligatory for the detaining authority to specify the date of the commencement of detention in the order.
why_respondent_won: The state's authority to continue the detention was upheld because, under Article 357(2) of the Constitution, the law under which the detention was ordered remained valid despite the revocation of the President's Proclamation.

The grounds for detention were deemed valid because the petitioner's possession of high explosive bombs, an offence under the Explosive Substances Act, and a prior incident of bomb-throwing clearly brought the case within the ambit of Section 3(2)(d) of the Act, which defines such acts as prejudicial to the maintenance of public order.

The court accepted the interpretation that Section 10's reference to the "date of detention" means the date a person is actually taken into custody, not a date that must be pre-emptively written into the detention order.
policy_considerations: As the object of detention is to prevent the detenu from acting in any manner prejudicial to the security of the State or the maintenance of public order, the grounds of detention supplied to the petitioner, in our opinion, should be held to be germane to the purpose for which detention order can legally be made under the Act.
